source_text: Coronant et publicos ordines laureis publicae caussae, magistratus vero insuper aureis. Superferuntur etiam illis Hetruscae. Hoc vocabulum est coronarum, quas gemmis et foliis ex auro quercinis ob Jovem insignis ad deducendas thensas cum palmatis togis sumunt. Sunt et provinciales aureae, imaginum jam, non virorum, capita majora quaerentes. Sed tui ordines et tui magistratus, et ipsum curiae nomen Ecclesia est Christi. Illius es conscriptus in libris vitae. Illic purpurae tuae sanguis Domini et clavus latus in cruce ipsius; illic securis ad caudicem arboris posita, illic virgae ex Jesse. Viderint et publici equi cum coronis suis. Dominus tuus, ubi secundum Scripturam Jerusalem ingredi voluit, nec asinum habuit privatum. Isti in curribus et isti in equis, nos autem in nomine Domini Dei nostri invocabimus. Ab ipso incolatu Babylonis illius in Apocalypsi Joannis submovemur, nedum a suggestu. Coronatur et vulgus nunc ex principalium prosperitatum exultatione, nunc ex municipalium solemnitatum proprietate: et est omnis publicae laetitiae luxuria captatrix. Sed tu peregrinus mundi hujus, civis supernae Jerusalem. Noster, inquit, municipatus in coelis. Habes tuos sensus, tuos fastos: nihil tibi cum gaudiis saeculi; imo contrarium debes: Saeculum enim gaudebit, vos vero lugebitis. Et puto, felices ait lugentes, non coronatos. Coronant et nuptiae sponsos, ideo non nubamus ethnicis, ne nos ad idolatriam usque deducant, a qua apud illos nuptiae incipiunt: habes legem a Patriarchis quidem, habes apostolum in Domino nubere jubentem. Coronat et libertas saecularis. Sed tu jam redemptus es a Christo, et quidem magno. Servum alienum quomodo saeculum manumittet? Etsi libertas videtur, sed et servitus videbatur. Omnia imaginaria in saeculo, et nihil veri. Nam et tunc liber hominis eras redemptus a Christo: et nunc servus es Christi, licet manumissus ab homine. Si veram putes saeculi libertatem, ut et corona consignes, rediisti in servitutem hominis, quam putes libertatem; amisisti libertatem Christi, quam putas servitutem. Numquid et agonisticae caussae disputabuntur, quas statim tituli sui damnant? et sacras et funebres scilicet, hoc enim superest ut Olympius Jupiter, et Nemaeus Hercules, et misellus Archemorus, et Antinous infelix in Christiano coronentur, ut ipse spectaculum fiat, quod spectare debet. Universas, ut arbitror, caussas enumeravimus. Nec ulla nobiscum est: omnes alienae, profanae, illicitae, semel jam in sacramenti testatione ejeratae. Haec enim erant pompae diaboli et angelorum ejus officia, saeculi honores, solemnitates, popularitates, falsa vota, humana servitia, laudes vanae, gloriae turpes: et in omnibus istis idololatria, in solo quoque sensu coronarum quibus omnia ista redimita sunt. Praefabitur quidem Claudius etiam coelum sideribus apud Homeri carmina coronatum; certe a Deo, certe homini, igitur et homo ipse a Deo coronandus est. Caeterum a saeculo coronantur et lupanaria, et latrinae, et pistrina, et carcer, et ludus, et ipsa amphitheatra, et ipsa spoliaria, ipsaeque libitinae. Quam sacer sanctus, quamque honestus ac mundus sit habitus iste, noli de uno poetico coelo, sed de totius mundi commerciis aestimare. At enim Christianus nec januam suam laureis infamabit, si norit quantos deos etiam ostiis diabolus affinxerit, Janum a janua, Limentinum a limine, Forculum et Cardam a foribus et cardinibus et apud Graecos Thyreum Apollinem et Antelios daemonas.
pass_a_gloss: They crown also public orders with laurels for public causes, but magistrates indeed with golden ones. Also Etruscan things are placed upon them. This word is of crowns, which with gems and leaves of oak from gold, notable because of Jupiter, they take for leading out processions with palmated togas. There are also provincial golden ones, now seeking larger heads of images, not of men. But your orders and your magistrates, and the very name of the senate, is the Church of Christ. You are enrolled in the books of life of Him. There your purple is the blood of the Lord and the nail in the side on the cross of Him; there the axe is placed at the trunk of the tree, there the rods from Jesse. Let them see also the public horses with their crowns. Your Lord, where He wished to enter Jerusalem according to Scripture, did not have a private donkey. These are in chariots and these on horses, but we will invoke in the name of the Lord our God. We are removed from the very dwelling of that Babylon in the Apocalypse of John, not to mention the tribunal. The crowd is also crowned now from the exultation of principal prosperities, now from the property of municipal solemnities: and all luxury of public joy is captivating. But you are a stranger of this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. Our municipality, it says, is in the heavens. You have your own senses, your own festivals: you have nothing to do with the joys of the age; indeed you owe the opposite: for the age will rejoice, but you will mourn. And I think, He says, blessed are those mourning, not those crowned. Weddings also crown the betrothed, therefore we do not marry pagans, lest they lead us to idolatry, from which weddings begin among them: you have the law from the Patriarchs, you have the apostle commanding to marry in the Lord. Secular freedom also crowns. But you have already been redeemed by Christ, and indeed at a great price. How will the secular world free a foreign slave? Even if freedom seems to be, yet slavery also seemed. All things in the age are imaginary, and nothing is true. For even then you were a free man redeemed by Christ: and now you are a slave of Christ, although freed by man. If you think the freedom of the age is true, so that you also ratify the crown, you have returned to the slavery of man, which you think is freedom; you have lost the freedom of Christ, which you think is slavery. Will perhaps also agonistic causes be disputed, which their own titles immediately condemn? And sacred and funeral ones, of course, for this remains, that Olympian Jupiter, and Nemean Hercules, and wretched Archemorus, and unhappy Antinous be crowned in a Christian, so that he himself becomes a spectacle, which he ought to watch. I think we have enumerated all causes. And none of them is with us: all are foreign, profane, illicit, having been once for all rejected in the testimony of the sacrament. For these were the pomp of the devil and the offices of his angels, the honors of the age, solemnities, popularities, false vows, human services, empty praises, shameful glories: and in all these things idolatry, in the very sense of crowns with which all these things are adorned. Claudius indeed also crowns the heaven with stars in the songs of Homer; certainly by God, certainly by man, therefore man himself is also to be crowned by God. Meanwhile, the age crowns also brothels, and latrines, and bakeries, and prison, and game, and the very amphitheaters, and the very spoliariums, and the very funeral processions. How sacred, how holy and clean is this habit, do not estimate from one poetic heaven, but from the commerce of the whole world. But indeed a Christian will not defile his door with laurels, if he knows how many gods the devil has also fixed on doors, Janus on the door, Limentinus on the threshold, Forculus and Cardus on the doors and hinges, and among the Greeks, Thyreus Apollo and Antelios demons.

pass_b_english: Public orders are crowned with laurels for public causes, magistrates with gold; Etruscan insignia are laid on top of them. The word means crowns set with gems and gold oak leaves, marked for Jupiter, worn when officials in palm-embroidered togas lead out the sacred processions. Provincial gold crowns also exist, now seeking larger heads for statues rather than men. But your orders, your magistrates, and the very name of the senate is the Church of Christ. You are enrolled in the books of his life. There your purple is the Lord's blood and the spear-wound in his cross; there the axe lies at the tree's trunk, there the rods from Jesse. Let them look at the public horses wearing their own crowns. When your Lord wished to enter Jerusalem according to Scripture, he did not even have a donkey of his own (Matthew 21:5). Those men ride in chariots and on horses, but we will call on the name of the Lord our God. We have been removed from the very dwelling of that Babylon in the Apocalypse of John, let alone the tribunal (Revelation 18:4). The crowd is crowned now from the exultation of imperial victories, now from the splendor of municipal festivals — every luxury of public joy is a trap. But you are a stranger in this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. "Our municipality," he says, "is in the heavens." You have your own senses, your own calendar; you have nothing to do with the age's joys — indeed you owe the opposite: the age will rejoice, but you will mourn. And I think he calls blessed those who mourn, not those who are crowned. Weddings crown the betrothed, which is why we do not marry pagans, lest they drag us into idolatry — since their weddings begin with it. You have the law from the Patriarchs, you have the apostle commanding marriage in the Lord. Secular freedom also crowns. But you have already been redeemed by Christ, and at a great price. How can the world free a slave who belongs to another? Even if freedom appears, slavery also once appeared. Everything in the age is imaginary, nothing true. For even then you were a free man redeemed by Christ; now you are Christ's slave, though freed by a man. If you think the world's freedom is true, so that you also ratify the crown, you have returned to the slavery of man, which you mistake for freedom; you have lost the freedom of Christ, which you mistake for slavery. Will agonistic causes also be debated — causes their own titles condemn at once? Sacred and funeral ones too, of course, since all that remains is for Olympian Jupiter, Nemean Hercules, wretched Archemorus, and unhappy Antinous to be crowned on a Christian, so that he becomes the spectacle he ought to be watching. I think we have enumerated every cause. None belongs to us; all are foreign, profane, illicit, rejected once for all in the testimony of the sacrament. These were the pomp of the devil and the offices of his angels: the age's honors, solemnities, popularities, false vows, human services, empty praises, shameful glories — and in all of them idolatry, in the very sense of the crowns with which all these things are adorned. Claudius indeed crowns heaven with stars in Homer's songs; certainly by God, certainly by man — therefore man himself is also to be crowned by God. Meanwhile the age crowns brothels, latrines, bakeries, prison, the game, the amphitheaters, the spoliariums, and funeral processions. How sacred, how holy and clean this habit is — do not judge it from one poetic heaven, but from the commerce of the whole world. But a Christian will not defile his door with laurels, if he knows how many gods the devil has fixed on doorways: Janus on the door, Limentinus on the threshold, Forculus and Cardus on the doors and hinges, and among the Greeks, Thyreus Apollo and Antelios demons.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that correctly interprets the theological and historical context (e.g., 'clavus latus' as 'spear-wound' and 'suggestu' as 'tribunal' in the context of Babylon's fall). Scripture citations added in Pass B (Matthew 21:5 and Revelation 18:4) are appropriate identifications of the alluded passages.

The Latin text is accurately translated in the English version. The translation preserves the meaning, structure, and theological nuances of the original. All key terms are rendered appropriately, and the scriptural citations are correctly matched to the text. The title 'The Christian and Crowns' accurately reflects the content of the passage. No omissions, additions, or distortions are present in the translation.
